newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish reactions vary after first summit reports.
newsitem.headline: Polish reactions vary after first summit reports.

text.p: Poland's President Aleksander Kwasniewski said that, at the Helsinki summit between U.S. leader Bill Clinton and Russia's Boris Yeltsin on Friday, Moscow had de facto agreed to NATO's expansion.

"I think that in this basic question, in fact, I stress in fact, Russia has agreed on the expansion of NATO," Kwasniewski said in an initial statement issued to Reuters by his spokesman Antoni Styrczula soon after the summit ended.
But senior opposition parliamentarian Janusz Onyszkiewicz said Polish diplomats should seek rapid clarification from NATO and Washington about what exactly had been agreed in the talks.
"The question now arises, what will NATO be and will it be an organisation which we would want to join," PAP news agency quoted him as saying during a break in parliamentary voting.

"Poland should not be interested in joining a diluted alliance whose effectiveness and credibility are not the same as hitherto," the former defence minister told PAP after first, sketchy reports of the summit's outcome.
The head of parliament's foreign affairs committee, opposition leader Bronislaw Geremek, told the agency however that news media may have misreported the summit's results.
"So far nothing bad has happened. The principle that "nothing (should be decided) about us without us' has not been violated," Geremek told PAP.
Warsaw has been anxious that NATO should not agree on a watered-down membership for new entrants, so as to meet Russian objections that the pact's enlargement threatens its security.
Kwasniewski said Poland had not raised objections to the readiness of the United States and NATO countries to sign a special charter with Russia.
"We think that, for a lasting system of security in Europe, such a charter between an expanded NATO and Russia and Ukraine can be very useful," Kwasniewski said in the initial comments.
"We also have the impression there was a drawing closer of standpoints and that in fact the expansion of NATO is decided," Kwasniewski said.
Poland expects to be among the first new members, with Hungary and the Czech Republic, to be asked at the pact's July summit in Madrid to start NATO entry talks and to join in 1999.
The country was left by its Western allies to domination by the Soviet Union at the end of World War Two and only threw this off in 1989.
Kwasniewski said he did not consider that Poland would be a second-class member of NATO because the Western pact did not intend to station nuclear weapons or forces on its territory.

"Denmark has a similar situation and no one regards it as a second-class member in NATO," he said, adding that there was no need for such measures now that the world had left behind the past conflict between great power blocs.

"In my view the presence of new countries in NATO is based on the same Washington treaty in which is included a clear assertion concerning security guarantees, mutual relations between countries of NATO, responsibility for the entirety of security in this region and cooperation in commanding these armies jointly," he said.
"So in my view the enlargement of NATO in peaceful conditions is expansion in which the presence of foreign armies and nuclear weapons is not essential," he said.
